title: SupTech: Mapping the Use of Technology in Financial Supervision
key_claim: IOSCO's first global SupTech survey of 49 securities authorities, accounting for over 75 percent of total global securities market value, finds SupTech is no longer experimental: 92 percent cite efficiency as a demand-side driver, 65 percent cite AI applications as a supply-side driver, and 51 percent have a dedicated SupTech budget.
frame_summary: Argues that supervisory technology has crossed from experimentation into consolidation and is now embedded in core supervisory functions, while cautioning that ambition still outruns funding and capability.
verbatim_list: With 49 authorities participating across all IOSCO regions, the survey provides a global snapshot of how technology is reshaping financial supervision.
Fifty-one percent of authorities indicate they have established a dedicated SupTech budget (Figure 11).
Eighty-six percent of respondents identified cyber risk as either high or critical in the context of SupTech implementation, making it the most prominent concern by a wide margin (Figure 7).
notes: The strongest in-window Tier 1 anchor: a standard-setter's own survey evidence that detection and analysis capability is being built into the supervisory core across 49 jurisdictions.

title: HMRC's annual report and accounts 2025 to 2026: Executive summary
key_claim: HMRC reports raising tax revenues of £966.4 billion in 2025-26 and over £50 billion of compliance yield for the first time, states that AI and advanced analytics enabled the protection and recovery of £10 billion in tax in the year, appointed its first Chief AI Officer in April 2026, and has increased compliance colleagues by over 2,100 since Autumn Budget 2024.
frame_summary: Presents detection and analytics capability, rather than new tax law, as the operational engine of tax-gap closure, framing technology and headcount investment as the route to higher effective enforcement.
verbatim_quote: In 2025 to 2026, we raised tax revenues of £966.4 billion, an increase of £90.4 billion compared to the previous year and brought in over £50 billion of compliance yield for the first time
verbatim_list: advanced analytics has already enabled the protection and recovery of £10 billion in tax between 2025 and 2026
To do this, we're employing innovative new technologies and capabilities, and have increased the number of compliance colleagues by over 2,100 since Autumn Budget 2024.
We are ahead of our plan to grow compliance capacity by an additional 5,500 new frontline compliance officers by 2030.
notes: The hardest single official number tying recovered revenue to analytics capability rather than to rule changes. The GOV.UK page renders acronyms inline (AI becomes 'AI (Artificial intelligence)'), so the £10 billion sentence is used as a figure via the body and not as a verbatim_quote string.

title: Simplifying EU rules to support competitiveness
key_claim: With two further omnibus proposals presented on 24 June 2026, the Commission has now tabled 12 omnibus simplification packages, which it says translate to EUR 18 billion in annual administrative savings, against a 2029 target of cutting burden by at least 25 percent for all businesses and 35 percent for SMEs.
frame_summary: Argues that the EU's competitiveness answer is to cut administrative burden and paperwork rather than to lower substantive standards, explicitly claiming that high social, environmental and consumer protections are maintained.
verbatim_quote: With these two new proposals, the Commission has presented 12 omnibus proposals across multiple sectors.
verbatim_list: These measures translate to €18 billion in annual administrative savings.
notes: Anchors the visible half of the signal: rule books are being simplified and deferred in public at the same moment supervisory detection capability is being built out quietly.

title: Artificial Intelligence: IRS Actions Needed to Address Skills Gaps, Information Quality, and Strategic Management
date_evidence: GAO-26-107522 Published: Mar 24, 2026. Publicly Released: Mar 24, 2026.
key_claim: The IRS held 126 active AI use cases as of June 2025, up from 10 in August 2022, most categorised as improving operational efficiency or tax compliance and fraud detection, with 61 percent still in development and 65 either too sensitive for public reporting or exempt as research and development. The agency lost 63 employees who had been working on AI.
frame_summary: Argues that the detection-oriented AI build-out inside a major tax authority is real and rapid but is outrunning its workforce, inventory quality and strategic management, so the capability may not deliver what the agency assumes.
verbatim_quote: IRS had 126 active artificial intelligence (AI) use cases—applications of AI for a particular business need—in its inventory as of June 2025.
verbatim_list: Although IRS has been using AI for several years, its inventory has grown rapidly since reporting 10 use cases in August 2022.
For example, officials in the Research, Applied Analytics and Statistics group said they lost 63 employees who had been working full- or part-time on AI.
notes: The single permitted structural anchor. Canonical primary document quantifying the detection-capability build inside a tax authority over time; no in-window document carries that series. Doubles as counter-evidence on capacity.

title: Deloitte's 2026 Global Tax Policy Survey finds rising tide of compliance and complexity is the biggest tax challenge facing global businesses
key_claim: A survey of 1,010 tax and finance leaders across 28 jurisdictions finds corporate expectation that e-invoicing will simplify compliance has fallen from 59 percent in 2024 to 36 percent in 2026, while almost 40 percent name increased compliance, administrative and reporting requirements as the biggest impact on their business.
frame_summary: Argues from the regulated side that digitalising tax administration is delivering more visibility and more burden rather than the promised simplification, so official simplification rhetoric and lived compliance experience are diverging.
verbatim_quote: In 2024, 59% of respondents expected it to deliver simplified compliance and fell to 36% in 2026.
verbatim_list: Deloitte's 2026 Global Tax Policy Survey of 1,010 tax and finance leaders across 28 jurisdictions reveals that organizations are facing increased tax complexity, growing compliance burdens and high upfront costs to reap the benefits of digitalization.
For almost 40% of respondents, increased compliance, administrative and reporting requirements are having the biggest impact on their business across all key areas of global tax policy surveyed.
notes: The demand-side mirror: firms report rising effective stringency at the same moment governments announce burden reduction.

title: The best spent money in Whitehall?
key_claim: Despite record compliance yield, HMRC carried out 306,000 compliance checks in 2025-26, down from 333,000 and below the 361,000 undertaken before the pandemic, prosecuted 300 tax fraud cases, and saw cash expected fall from £14.2 billion to £12.1 billion; upstream estimated yield now accounts for 42 percent of the total, against 29 percent five years ago.
frame_summary: Argues that the headline enforcement success story is increasingly composed of modelled prevention rather than observed detection, and that actual pursuit of non-compliant taxpayers is falling even as the tax gap grows.
verbatim_quote: HMRC carried out 306,000 compliance checks in 2025-26, down from 333,000 the previous year and still well below the 361,000 undertaken before the pandemic.
verbatim_list: This ‘upstream’ effort now accounts for 42 percent of HMRC's compliance yield, compared with 29 percent five years ago.
Annual "cash expected" from compliance activity fell from £14.2 billion in 2024-25 to £12.1 billion in 2025-26.
notes: The counter-argument source. Interrogates the same HMRC accounts and reaches the opposite conclusion about detection probability.

title: Researchers link IRS staffing cuts, reporting gaps to weaker compliance
key_claim: Research presented at the 16th IRS/TPC Joint Research Conference on 25 June 2026 documents a visibility gradient in which net misreporting is 1 percent for income subject to substantial information reporting and withholding but 55 percent for income with little or none, and finds an 11 percent IRS workforce reduction cut tax filings by 3.2 percent in affected states.
frame_summary: Argues that the tax gap is primarily an information-architecture problem, determined by how much of a taxpayer's activity is already visible to the authority, rather than by enforcement effort or taxpayer morality alone.
verbatim_quote: Net misreporting is lowest, at 1%, for income subject to substantial information reporting and withholding, such as wages.
verbatim_list: It is highest, at 55%, for income with little or no information reporting.
The study found that states more affected by the cuts saw a 3.2% decrease in tax filings.
notes: The cleanest quantified proof of the mechanism: visibility, not rule stringency, determines compliance. Also supplies counter-evidence that detection capacity can fall.

title: Cyber risks and resource constraints impeding SupTech take-up: IOSCO survey
key_claim: Reports IOSCO's SupTech survey alongside a separate 87-page Supervisory Toolkit for AI Use in Capital Markets published on 25 May 2026, and notes that funding gaps are slowing progress against strong high-tech ambitions.
frame_summary: Argues that supervisory AI adoption is now a coordinated international programme with a visible institutional calendar, but that funding gaps and cyber exposure are throttling deployment speed.
verbatim_quote: IOSCO last month (25 May) published an 87-page 'Supervisory Toolkit for AI Use in Capital Markets'.
notes: Independent corroboration of the IOSCO publication date and evidence that the detection build-out is a programme rather than a single report.
